paper_description: This paper presents an optimal spin-lock priority assignment (OSPA) algorithm for real-time multi-core systems using partitioned fixed-priority preemptive scheduling (P-FPPS). It introduces a generalized worst-case response-time analysis for arbitrary fixed per-core spin-lock priorities and an algorithm to find an optimal spin-lock priority per core that maximizes schedulability. The OSPA algorithm aims to find a spin-lock priority assignment that makes a task set schedulable if such an assignment exists.

formal_description.statement: For any global resource R_q, the minimum resource holding time on any core P_r is when \pi_{spin}^{P_k} = \pi_{max}^{P_k}, which is the spin-lock priority used by HP.

variables.\\pi_{spin}^{P_k}: The spin-lock priority on processor P_k
variables.\\pi_{max}^{P_k}: The highest priority level on processor P_k
variables.RHT_{r,q}: Maximum holding time of R_q by all tasks on processor P_r

assumptions: Non-nested and non-preemptive global resource access
The formula for RHT_{r,q} is given by (24) in the paper.
formal_description.conclusion: The minimum resource holding time for a global resource R_q on a core P_r occurs when the spin-lock priority on that core is set to the highest possible priority (\pi_{max}^{P_k}).

informal_sketch.intuition: To minimize how long a resource is held on a core, we want to ensure that only the tasks that absolutely must hold it, and only for their necessary duration, do so. Setting the spin-lock priority to the highest level on a core effectively restricts which tasks can potentially contribute to the resource holding time, thereby minimizing it.
steps: Consider the formula for RHT_{r,q} (Equation 24 in the paper). This formula calculates the maximum holding time of resource R_q on processor P_r.
Analyze Equation 24 under different spin-lock priorities \pi_{spin}^{P_r}.

When \pi_{spin}^{P_r} = \pi_{max}^{P_r} (the HP case), Equation 24 simplifies. Since there are no tasks with priorities higher than \pi_{max}^{P_r}, only tasks with priorities less than or equal to \pi_{max}^{P_r} can contribute to RHT_{r,q}.

In this scenario (\pi_{spin}^{P_r} = \pi_{max}^{P_r}), the formula for RHT_{r,q} effectively becomes the maximum resource access time among tasks on P_r for holding R_q, as only one task from the set of tasks with priority \le \pi_{spin}^{P_r} can hold the resource at a time.

For any \pi_{spin}^{P_r} < \pi_{max}^{P_r}, tasks with priorities higher than \pi_{spin}^{P_r} can still contribute to RHT_{r,q} (as per Equation 25). This potentially increases the resource holding time compared to the \pi_{spin}^{P_r} = \pi_{max}^{P_r} case.
Therefore, the minimum RHT_{r,q} is achieved when \pi_{spin}^{P_r} = \pi_{max}^{P_r}.
key_insights: The highest spin-lock priority on a core minimizes the set of tasks that can contribute to resource holding time.
This minimization is achieved by preventing higher-priority tasks (relative to the spin-lock priority) from interfering with the resource acquisition of lower-priority tasks that are spinning.

formal_description.statement: A task \tau_i \in T_{P_k} does not experience any delay due to spinning of local higher and lower priority tasks when \pi_{spin}^{P_k} < \pi_i, whereas, in the worst-case, it experiences delay due to both spinning of local higher and lower priority tasks that use global resources when \pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i.

variables.T_{P_k}: Set of tasks on processor P_k

assumptions: The analysis considers two cases based on the relationship between \pi_i and \pi_{spin}^{P_k}.
The paper refers to Figure 1 for priority ranges (LtLs, LtELs, LtHs, HtHs, HtELs).
formal_description.conclusion: The impact of spinning by other local tasks on a task's response time depends on the relationship between the task's priority and the core's spin-lock priority.

informal_sketch.intuition: When a task spins for a resource, its priority is temporarily raised. This can affect other tasks. This lemma clarifies when spinning by other tasks (higher or lower priority) will or will not cause delays to the spinning task itself.
steps: Consider the case where \pi_{spin}^{P_k} < \pi_i (Case 2 in the paper). In this scenario, task \tau_i has a priority higher than the spin-lock priority.
When \tau_i spins, its priority is raised to \pi_{spin}^{P_k}. Since \pi_{spin}^{P_k} < \pi_i, \tau_i can still preempt any task with priority lower than \pi_i.

Crucially, tasks with priorities higher than \pi_i (HtHs range) can preempt \tau_i even when \tau_i is spinning at \pi_{spin}^{P_k}. However, the paper states that \tau_i does not experience delay from these higher priority tasks' spinning in this case (referencing Equation 26).

Similarly, tasks with priorities lower than \pi_i but higher than \pi_{spin}^{P_k} (LtHs range) can preempt \tau_i. However, the paper indicates that \tau_i does not experience delay from these lower priority tasks' spinning in this case (referencing Equation 11 which doesn't include spin-lock time from lower priority tasks).
Now consider the case where \pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i (Case 1 in the paper). In this scenario, task \tau_i has a priority lower than or equal to the spin-lock priority.
When \tau_i spins, its priority is raised to \pi_{spin}^{P_k}. This prevents any task with priority lower than \pi_{spin}^{P_k} from preempting it.

Tasks with priorities higher than \pi_i but lower than or equal to \pi_{spin}^{P_k} (LtLs, LtELs ranges in Figure 1.a) can preempt \tau_i. The paper states that \tau_i experiences delay due to spinning of these lower priority tasks (referencing Equation 6).

Tasks with priorities higher than \pi_{spin}^{P_k} (HtHs, HtELs ranges in Figure 1.a) can also preempt \tau_i. The paper states that \tau_i experiences delay due to spinning of these higher priority tasks (referencing Equation 26).
Therefore, when \pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i, \tau_i can be delayed by both higher and lower priority tasks that are spinning.
key_insights: The relationship between a task's priority and the core's spin-lock priority dictates which other tasks' spinning can cause delays.
When a task's priority is higher than the spin-lock priority, it is less susceptible to delays from other tasks' spinning.

formal_description.statement: A task \tau_i \in T_{P_k}, in the worst-case, experiences multiple pi-blocking from lower priority tasks that have a priority higher than the spin-lock priority and induced jitter due to suspension of higher priority tasks when \pi_{spin}^{P_k} < \pi_i, while such delays are not incurred to \tau_i when \pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i.

variables.T_{P_k}: Set of tasks on processor P_k

assumptions: The analysis considers two cases based on the relationship between \pi_i and \pi_{spin}^{P_k}.
The paper refers to Figure 1 for priority ranges.
formal_description.conclusion: When a task's priority is higher than the spin-lock priority, it is more susceptible to pi-blocking from lower-priority tasks and jitter from higher-priority task suspensions. These delays are avoided when the task's priority is lower than or equal to the spin-lock priority.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma focuses on the 'local' delays (pi-blocking and jitter) that a task experiences. It highlights that when a task has a higher priority than the spin-lock priority, it's more vulnerable to these types of delays from other tasks.
steps: Consider the case where \pi_{spin}^{P_k} < \pi_i (Case 2 in the paper). Here, \tau_i has a priority higher than the spin-lock priority.

The paper states that \tau_i experiences multiple pi-blocking from lower priority tasks that have a priority higher than \pi_{spin}^{P_k} (tasks in the LtHs range). This is quantified by Equation (20) and (13). This is because \tau_i spins at a priority lower than these tasks, allowing them to preempt and potentially block \tau_i.

Additionally, \tau_i may experience induced jitter due to suspension of higher priority tasks (as described in Section V-D and Equation 17). This jitter arises when higher priority tasks suspend themselves to access global resources.
Now consider the case where \pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i (Case 1 in the paper). Here, \tau_i has a priority lower than or equal to the spin-lock priority.
In this case, \tau_i spins at a priority \pi_{spin}^{P_k} which is higher than or equal to its own priority \pi_i. This prevents lower priority tasks from preempting it and causing pi-blocking.
Furthermore, the induced jitter from higher priority task suspensions is not incurred to \tau_i when \pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i, as per the analysis in Section V-D.
Therefore, the specific delays mentioned (multiple pi-blocking from tasks with priority > \pi_{spin}^{P_k} and jitter from higher priority suspensions) are present in Case 2 but absent in Case 1.
key_insights: The spin-lock priority acts as a shield against certain types of local blocking.
When a task's priority is lower than or equal to the spin-lock priority, it is better protected from pi-blocking by lower-priority tasks and jitter from higher-priority tasks.

formal_description.statement: The maximum incurred local delay to a task \tau_i \in T_{P_k} may decrease if the spin-lock priority is lower than the priority of the task, i.e., from Case (1) (\pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i) to Case (2) (\pi_{spin}^{P_k} < \pi_i), provided that the reduction in spinning delays outweighs the increase in pi-blocking and jitter.

variables.T_{P_k}: Set of tasks on processor P_k
variables.Local Delay: Sum of pi-blocking and spinning delays

assumptions: The analysis considers two cases: \pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i (Case 1) and \pi_{spin}^{P_k} < \pi_i (Case 2).
Corollaries 1 and 2 are used in the proof.
formal_description.conclusion: Lowering the spin-lock priority below a task's own priority can potentially reduce the task's total local delay (spinning + pi-blocking), but this is contingent on the trade-off between reduced spinning delays and increased pi-blocking/jitter.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma explores the trade-off when we lower the spin-lock priority. It suggests that this might be beneficial for a task's local delay, but it comes at the cost of increased pi-blocking and jitter. The net effect depends on which cost is higher.
steps: Recall Corollaries 1 and 2. They describe the delays incurred in Case 1 (\pi_{spin}^{P_k} \ge \pi_i) and Case 2 (\pi_{spin}^{P_k} < \pi_i).
In Case 1, \tau_i experiences delays due to spinning of both higher and lower priority tasks (from Corollary 1).
In Case 2, the delays due to spinning of higher and lower priority tasks are removed (from Corollary 1).
However, in Case 2, \tau_i incurs additional pi-blocking from lower priority tasks (with priority > \pi_{spin}^{P_k}) and jitter from higher priority task suspensions (from Corollary 2).
The lemma states that the maximum incurred local delay to \tau_i *may* decrease when moving from Case 1 to Case 2.

This decrease happens if the reduction in spinning delays (which is significant when moving from Case 1 to Case 2) is greater than the increase in pi-blocking and jitter (which also occurs when moving from Case 1 to Case 2).
Therefore, lowering the spin-lock priority below \pi_i can be beneficial if the reduction in spinning delays is more substantial than the added pi-blocking and jitter.
key_insights: There's a trade-off between spinning delays and pi-blocking/jitter when adjusting the spin-lock priority.
Lowering the spin-lock priority can be advantageous if the reduction in spinning delays is the dominant factor.

formal_description.statement: The presented Optimal Spin-Lock Priority Assignment (OSPA) algorithm (Algorithm 1) is optimal. If there exists a fixed spin-lock priority per core that can make the system schedulable based on the analysis presented in Section V, the OSPA algorithm will find it.
assumptions: Non-nested and non-preemptive global resource access
The schedulability analysis presented in Section V is accurate and used by the algorithm.
formal_description.conclusion: The OSPA algorithm is guaranteed to find a schedulable spin-lock priority assignment if one exists.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is the core claim of the paper. It states that the proposed algorithm is exhaustive and will find a solution if one is possible. The algorithm systematically explores spin-lock priorities, and this theorem proves that this exploration is sufficient.
steps: The OSPA algorithm starts by setting all spin-lock priorities to the highest possible value (HP-like behavior) on each core.
It then iteratively checks the schedulability of all tasks on all cores.
If any task on a core P_k is unschedulable, the algorithm lowers the spin-lock priority on that core to one priority level below the lowest priority task that missed its deadline.
This lowering of the spin-lock priority is guided by Lemma 2, which suggests that lowering the spin-lock priority below a task's priority can potentially reduce local delays.
The algorithm continues this process, reducing the spin-lock priority on each core until either all tasks are schedulable or the lowest possible spin-lock priority (LP-like behavior) is reached.
The algorithm terminates and returns success if a schedulable assignment is found.

If, at any point, lowering the spin-lock priority causes a task that was previously schedulable to become unschedulable, and this task has a priority higher than the new spin-lock priority, the algorithm declares failure (as per lines 10-12 of Algorithm 1). This is a crucial part of ensuring optimality by not overlooking potential issues caused by priority inversions.

The proof of optimality relies on the fact that the algorithm explores the space of spin-lock priorities in a way that guarantees it will find a schedulable configuration if one exists. This is supported by the lemmas that analyze the impact of spin-lock priority on different types of delays (spinning, pi-blocking, jitter).

Specifically, the algorithm's iterative reduction of spin-lock priorities, combined with the analysis of how local and remote blocking change with \pi_{spin}^{P_k}, ensures that if a schedulable assignment exists, it will be discovered.
key_insights: The algorithm systematically explores the spin-lock priority space.
The lemmas provide the theoretical foundation for why this systematic exploration is sufficient to guarantee optimality.
The algorithm's termination condition and failure handling are designed to ensure that it doesn't miss a schedulable solution or incorrectly declare failure.
